pantheon.desc: Still a working building after nineteen centuries, and free to enter. Stand under the oculus rather than around the edges — the whole room is built to send your eye up through that hole in the roof.

navona.desc: Baroque theatre on the footprint of a Roman stadium, which is why it is long and rounded at one end. The cafés on the square charge for the view; the streets one block off do not.

santeustachio.desc: A standing-room coffee bar behind the Pantheon, famous enough to have a queue and quick enough that it never matters. Order at the till first, then hand the receipt across the counter.

campodefiori.desc: A morning market square that turns into a drinking square after dark. Come while the stalls are still up — produce, cheese and *porchetta* — and eat standing.

armando.desc: A small family-run Roman kitchen beside the Pantheon, doing the four classic pastas without reinventing them. Book: the room is tiny and turns over slowly.

sanluigi.desc: The French national church, and three Caravaggios in a side chapel that most visitors walk straight past. Bring coins for the light box, or wait for someone else to feed it.

colosseo.desc: The one that needs a booked slot and a decision about how deep to go — arena floor and underground are separate tickets. Early or late spares you both the queue and the sun.

forum.desc: Not a building but a whole flattened city centre, and it reads as rubble until you pick a route through it. The Palatine above is quieter and gives you the Forum from overhead.

capitoline.desc: The oldest public museum collection in the world, on the hill Michelangelo laid out. The bronze she-wolf and the colossal marble hand are here, and the terrace looks straight down the Forum.

campidoglio.desc: The balcony behind the Capitoline palaces, looking over the Forum with no ticket and no queue. Best at dusk, when the ruins light up and the day crowd has gone.

taverna.desc: A neighbourhood osteria on the Monti side of the Fori, doing Roman standards at Roman prices. Small, so an early sitting or a reservation.

trevi.desc: Far larger in person than photographs suggest, and wedged into a square too small for it. Go very early or very late; the middle of the day is shoulder to shoulder.

spanishsteps.desc: A staircase that works as a grandstand — sitting on the steps is no longer allowed, so treat it as a passage rather than a rest. The view back down Via Condotti is the point.

pincio.desc: The terrace above Piazza del Popolo, looking west across the rooftops to St Peter's dome. It is the standard Rome sunset, and it earns the reputation.

vaticanmus.desc: Hours of collection funnelling toward one ceiling, and the route is one-way. Book a slot, go at opening or late, and decide in advance what you are willing to walk past.

stpeters.desc: Free to enter, with a security queue that shapes the visit — go early. The dome climb is a separate ticket and the last stretch is a narrow, leaning staircase.

santangelo.desc: Hadrian's tomb, later a fortress and papal bolt-hole, with a spiral ramp climbing through the middle of it. The bridge in front is the best-dressed in the city.

smtrastevere.desc: One of the oldest churches in Rome, and the golden mosaics across the apse are what people come for. The square outside is the neighbourhood's living room.

trasteverewalk.desc: The point of Trastevere is not a monument but the grid — narrow, ivy-covered, washing overhead. Head east of Viale Trastevere for the quieter half.

sancalisto.desc: An unreconstructed neighbourhood bar on its own square: cheap coffee, cheaper beer, plastic chairs, all ages. Nothing is designed, which is the appeal.

trapizzino.desc: A pocket of pizza bianca filled with Roman stews — *pollo alla cacciatora*, oxtail — invented for exactly this kind of standing lunch. Two is a meal.

daenzo.desc: A tiny Trastevere trattoria with a long-standing reputation and a queue to match. No reservations for most sittings; go at opening or expect to wait.

gianicolo.desc: The hill above Trastevere, and the widest view in Rome — the whole centre laid out flat. A cannon is fired here at noon.

monti.desc: The village-in-the-city between the Forum and Termini: workshops, wine bars and a small square everyone sits in. Via Urbana and Via del Boschetto are the spine.

vincoli.desc: A plain church holding Michelangelo's *Moses*, carved for a papal tomb that was never finished at the scale intended. Ten minutes, and worth the climb up from the Colosseum.

maggiore.desc: One of the four great papal basilicas, with fifth-century mosaics running the length of the nave. Dress code applies, as at all of them.

panella.desc: A bakery and coffee counter on Via Merulana with a long display of Roman baking. Good for a pastry standing at the bar, or a sit-down breakfast outside.

mercatocentrale.desc: A food hall built into Termini station — a spread of small counters under one roof. Useful precisely because it is fast, open late and next to the trains.

orangegarden.desc: A walled orange grove on the Aventine with a terrace over the river and the dome. The keyhole in the priory gate next door frames St Peter's exactly; there is usually a short queue for it.

testacciomkt.desc: A modern covered market in a working neighbourhood, built for eating rather than sightseeing. Sandwich and pasta counters at the back; it winds down in the early afternoon.

bocca.desc: A drain cover carved as a face, in the portico of a church, with a queue for a photograph of a hand in its mouth. Five minutes — but the church behind it is genuinely old and quiet.

borghese.desc: A small, dense collection — Bernini's sculpture above all — in a villa that limits everyone to a strict two-hour slot. Must be booked ahead; entry is refused without one.

borghesepark.desc: The city's big central park, above the Spanish Steps: umbrella pines, a boating lake and long gravel avenues. Easiest as the way to or from the Galleria.

ostia.desc: Rome's harbour town, abandoned rather than destroyed, so streets, baths and apartment blocks still stand. A half-hour train from Porta San Paolo and a whole day once you are there.

popolo.desc: The old northern gate of the city, with twin churches framing the road in and two Caravaggios in Santa Maria del Popolo. The Pincio steps go up from the corner.

arapacis.desc: Augustus's altar of peace, sealed inside a modern glass box that is itself part of the argument. Small and quick, and the carved processional frieze repays standing close.

ghetto.desc: One of the oldest Jewish quarters in Europe, layered straight onto Roman ruins at the Portico d'Ottavia. Bakeries and *carciofi alla giudia*; read the brass stones underfoot.

isola.desc: A boat-shaped island mid-river, with a hospital, a church and the oldest bridge in Rome still in use. A short crossing rather than a destination — best at dusk.

caracalla.desc: Imperial baths on a scale that is hard to believe until you are inside the walls, and almost always empty compared to the Forum. Vaults gone, footprint intact.

giolitti.desc: A long-running gelateria near the Pantheon with a marble-counter routine: pay first, then order. Ask for panna and they will add it without charging.

stignazio.desc: A Jesuit church whose dome is painted flat on the ceiling — stand on the marker in the nave and it lifts. Free, small, and over in fifteen minutes.

trattoriamonti.desc: A family kitchen in Monti cooking from the Marche rather than Rome — the tortello with egg yolk is what it is known for. Book ahead; it is small and busy.
